newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore's Goh "furious" over U.S. criticism.
newsitem.headline: Singapore's Goh "furious" over U.S. criticism.

text.p: Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong said on Thursday he was "furious, flabbergasted and floored" over U.S. criticism of his election campaign tactics.

"I was astounded yesterday when I heard of this report...and I can tell you I was furious, I was flabbergasted, floored," Goh told reporters on the campaign trail for January 2 elections in which his People's Action Party (PAP) is assured of a majority.
"Yes, we have to respond officially," Goh said when asked if Singapore would respond to a U.S. State Department comment.
A State Department spokeswoman criticised Goh and other PAP candidates on Tuesday over their use of a housing upgrade programme to woo voters.

Goh and other ministers have told voters they would lose out on renovation schemes that would increase the value of their homes if they elected an opposition candidate. Goh said their housing estates would get left behind and become slums.
The PAP, which has won every election since 1959, was returned to power before a vote was cast when opposition parties declared they would contest only 36 of parliament's 83 seats.
"This is a local election and what we offer the people as a programme is no more different from what any candidate anywhere else will offer their electorate," Goh said.
"It is a program for the people and the people have the right to choose, to support my program or to reject it."
Goh said the State Department remarks were, "totally absurd and it took me 10 minutes to calm myself down before I could face the press conference".
He said that the government had to respond officially, "because this is not the same as (New York Times columnist Willam) Safire criticising me or criticising Senior Minister (Lee Kwan Yew).

"It is not the same as The Economist making fun of me. When the government gets into the act through the State Department, through a spokesman, at this stage when we have an election on warning us not to use such tactics, I think that is beyond their pale," he said.

The State Department said on Wednesday: "We understand that ruling party candidates, including the prime minister, have warned that constituencies that elect opposition candidates will receive low priority in extensive government plans to upgrade housing facilities."
"We believe that voters everywhere should be able to vote without fear of repercussions from government as a result of their resposibilities as citizens."

Goh said: "Maybe the motivation is we should practice the kind of democracy they practice. And we are practicing the kind of democary they practice in this case. Giving candidates their own free run to expound their programme and letting people decide."
Information Minister George Yeo joined in lambasting the U.S. comment.

"I am quite surprised that the Americans should raise an issue about how we run democratic politics in Singapore when their pork-barrel politics is something of a long tradition," he told state television.
Upgrading is not the only programme the PAP has tied to victory for its candidates. Goh outlined at a Monday news conference a lengthy list of community development schemes.

"The point couldn't be simpler: the government will implement these programmes in wards where their candidates are returned; they won't be implemented where PAP candidates are voted out," said a commentary in the Business Times newspaper.
The opposition won just four seats in the last parliament, but that was its best showing since Singapore's independence in 1965.
